title: Who gives amrit
hook: five amritdhari Sikhs, with a sixth attending the Granth

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Guru Panth: the gathered Khalsa, carrying the Guru's authority beside the Granth. Your line was the people as guru. Who did you ask before you decided, and did their answer change anything? Day one thousand two hundred seventy-two.

A door is closed. Not locked, just closed, so the room stays quiet. Inside, the Guru Granth Sahib rests open, and one Sikh sits beside it. Five more stand together, wearing the five Ks, washed and ready. Six people and the book. That's the whole staff. Nobody arrives from a head office. Nobody signs a certificate on behalf of an institution. Yesterday this path called the gathered Khalsa the Guru Panth, and it can sound like a big, abstract idea. The Sikh code shows what it looks like when it shrinks to the size of one room, on the day someone new is about to join. So, who gives amrit?
screen: `A CLOSED DOOR, A QUIET ROOM.` → `SIX PEOPLE AND THE BOOK.` → `WHO GIVES AMRIT?`

segments.voice: The Sikh Rehat Maryada answers plainly. In paraphrase: the initiation may be held in any quiet, suitable place. Besides the Guru Granth Sahib, six Sikhs need to be present. One attends the Granth. Five give the amrit. Start with the one. Their task is to sit in attendance on the Guru Granth Sahib, which Sikhs honor as the Guru present in the room. The ceremony doesn't happen while the book waits on a shelf. It happens in the Guru's presence, with someone caring for that presence the whole time. Then the five. The code asks that they be Sikhs who have taken amrit themselves, who keep the five Ks, and who live by the code. Put simply, you can only pass on what you have received. Nobody gives amrit on the strength of a title, a degree or a family name. The five give it because they already stand inside the promise they are about to offer. Now notice the number. The code asks for five, not one. Together they stand in for the panj pyare, the five beloved ones of Anandpur, whom this path met long ago. So the authority in the room doesn't belong to any single one of them. It sits between them. That's yesterday's Guru Panth, made small enough to fit behind a closed door. And the five are not a fixed set of people. Any five who meet the code's terms can be chosen for the day. Another month, another town, five different Sikhs, and the amrit is the same amrit. So the answer to who gives amrit isn't a single who. It's a five. The five give.
screen: `ANY QUIET PLACE, THE GRANTH PRESENT.` · `ONE SIKH ATTENDS THE GRANTH.` · `FIVE WHO HAVE TAKEN AMRIT THEMSELVES.` · `AUTHORITY SITS BETWEEN THE FIVE.` · then, large: `THE FIVE GIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture six quiet people. Settle, and let your breath slow down. See the room. The Granth open, one person seated beside it. Then five standing together, with no one in front of the others. Let your attention rest on each of the five in turn. You don't need faces; a shape is enough. Then bring to mind something good you have only ever received from a group: a team, a family table, a crew that covered for you once. Stay with that until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Who gives amrit. Five Sikhs who have taken amrit themselves give it together, while a sixth attends the Guru Granth Sahib. Today's word.
Your line: the five give. Today, pass on one thing you were given, a skill, a recipe, a kindness, to someone who hasn't received it yet. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: Under the Sikh Rehat Maryada, amrit is given in a quiet place in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib by five amritdhari Sikhs who keep the code, while a sixth Sikh attends the Granth.

what it means: five Sikhs who have taken amrit give it together, with a sixth attending the Guru Granth Sahib.
what a scholar hears: the code puts the authority in the five as a group, not in any single office or title.

sources.ref: Sikh Rehat Maryada, the amrit ceremony (Article XXIV)

notes: The requirements (any quiet, convenient place; the Guru Granth Sahib present; six Sikhs, one in attendance on the Granth and five to administer; the five being amritdhari, keeping the five Ks and of good conduct) are paraphrased from the Sikh Rehat Maryada's section on the amrit ceremony. Please confirm the article number and the paraphrase.
The script deliberately does not say whether women may be among the five; please advise whether the code's wording on this should be added.
The Guru receiving amrit from the first five is attributed to tradition; day 1271 told it the day before.
'Washed and ready' in the hook reflects the code's instruction that those administering bathe and wash their hair; please confirm.
